title: Hot Tub Running Costs in Australia: What to Budget in 2026
excerpt: Electricity, chemicals, water and servicing — here's what Aussie hot tub owners actually spend each year and how to cut those costs.
body:
Buying a hot tub is one thing; keeping it running is another. Many Australians are caught off guard by the ongoing costs after installation. This guide breaks down every regular expense you can expect in 2026, with realistic figures based on typical Australian conditions and energy prices.

## The Biggest Cost: Electricity

Electricity is almost always the dominant running cost for a hot tub. How much you spend depends on three things: your local electricity tariff, how often the spa is used, and how well the unit is insulated.

Australian electricity prices vary significantly by state, but a reasonable national average in 2026 sits around **30–35 cents per kWh** for a standard residential tariff. Most portable hot tubs draw between 1 kW and 3.5 kW depending on whether the heater and jets are running simultaneously.

A rough annual electricity estimate for a well-insulated 5–6 person spa used 3–4 times per week:

| Insulation Quality | Est. Annual Electricity Cost |
|---|---|
| Entry-level (thin foam) | $1,400 – $2,000 |
| Mid-range (full-foam) | $900 – $1,300 |
| Premium (multi-density foam + insulated cover) | $600 – $950 |

Full-foam insulation and a quality thermal cover make a measurable difference. If you're comparing models at point of purchase, ask for the CEC (Coefficient of Energy Consumption) rating — lower is better.

**Tip:** Running your spa on a time-of-use tariff and scheduling heating cycles during off-peak hours (typically late night to early morning) can shave 15–25% off your electricity bill.

## Water and Chemicals

A standard hot tub holds 1,000–1,500 litres. Most owners do a full drain and refill every 3–4 months, so you're looking at roughly 3–4 refills per year. At Sydney Water's 2026 residential rate, that's a negligible cost — water is rarely the issue.

Chemicals are where costs add up:

- **Sanitiser (chlorine or bromine):** $150–$300/year depending on usage and product type. Bromine suits hot water better and produces less odour, but costs slightly more.
- **pH adjusters (pH Up / pH Down):** $40–$80/year
- **Alkalinity increaser:** $30–$60/year
- **Shock treatment:** $60–$120/year
- **Spa-specific clarifier or enzyme products:** $50–$100/year

**Estimated annual chemical spend: $330–$660**

If you opt for a saltwater chlorinator or an ozone/UV system, upfront equipment costs are higher but ongoing chemical spend drops — typically by 40–60% on sanitiser.

## Servicing and Maintenance

Many owners service their own spas with basic testing and chemical dosing. Even so, budget for:

- **Filter cartridge replacement:** Filters should be replaced every 12–18 months depending on use. Replacement cartridges cost $30–$120 each depending on size and brand.
- **Professional service call (annual or bi-annual):** A qualified spa technician checking jets, seals, pumps and the heater element costs $120–$250 per visit. Worth it for the first year especially.
- **Cover replacement:** Spa covers degrade over 3–5 years in Australian UV conditions. Budget $300–$700 to replace when the foam becomes waterlogged.
- **Jet or seal repairs:** Minor leaks and cracked jet faces are common after 4–5 years. Budget a small contingency of $100–$200/year on average over the spa's lifespan.

## Total Annual Running Cost: A Realistic Summary

For a mid-range hot tub used regularly by an Australian household:

- Electricity: $900–$1,300
- Chemicals: $330–$660
- Filter and minor maintenance: $80–$150
- Amortised servicing and cover costs: $150–$250

**Total: roughly $1,460–$2,360 per year**, or $120–$200 per month.

High-end, well-insulated spas at the lower end of that range. Older or entry-level models at the higher end.

## How to Keep Costs Down Without Sacrificing Enjoyment

- **Buy a quality thermal cover and use it religiously.** Heat loss through the surface is massive if the cover is poor or left off.
- **Set the temperature to 36°C rather than 40°C** when the spa is used less frequently. Each degree costs energy to maintain.
- **Test water twice a week** and dose accurately — over-dosing chemicals is a common waste.
- **Clean the filter monthly** with a cartridge rinse. A blocked filter strains the pump and heater.
- **Ask your energy retailer about controlled load or off-peak rates** that suit heating cycles.

## Actionable Takeaway

Before buying any hot tub, ask the retailer for the unit's energy consumption data and factor in at least $1,500/year in running costs for a realistic budget. The difference in annual electricity costs between a poorly insulated entry-level spa and a quality full-foam model can easily exceed $600 — making the cheaper spa significantly more expensive over five years.
